item.title: Ruby Conf 12 - Y Not- Adventures in Functional Programming by Jim Weirich
item.description:
Confreaks · talk · intermediate · evergreen

Jim Weirich's RubyConf 2012 talk derives the Y combinator step by step, live-coding in Ruby lambdas. It builds up an understanding of functional programming and lambda calculus from first principles.

Why HN recommends it: HN recommends it repeatedly as one of the best and most entertaining programming talks, and as the talk that makes the Y combinator click, even for people who do not use Ruby.

“perhaps the most entertaining and interesting technical talk I've ever seen.” — HN comment, 2015

item.title: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
item.description:
Andrej Karpathy · lecture · intro · evergreen

Andrej Karpathy's first Neural Networks: Zero to Hero lecture, which builds micrograd, a tiny autograd engine, from scratch in Python. It explains backpropagation and neural network training step by step, assuming only basic Python and some high-school calculus.

Why HN recommends it: HN treats it as the best starting point for really understanding backprop and neural nets, because Karpathy explains the why with intuition and builds everything in code.

“It's especially useful because he explains the why and provides intuitive explanations instead of just talking about the what and how.” — HN comment, 2023

item.title: How Python was Shaped by leaky Internals, Armin Ronacher, Flask framework
item.description:
Видео с мероприятий {speach! · talk · advanced · evergreen

Armin Ronacher, creator of Flask, explains how CPython's internals and C API leak into the language's semantics. Using examples like the complexity of the add operation, he shows why Python is hard to optimize or reimplement.

Why HN recommends it: It is HN's standard answer to why Python cannot easily get much faster, and is recommended by people who work on JITs and alternative runtimes.

“This excellent talk describes how the semantics of the "add" operation are much more complex than generally described.” — HN comment, 2021

item.title: RailsConf 2014 - All the Little Things by Sandi Metz
item.description:
Confreaks · talk · intermediate · evergreen

Sandi Metz takes an ugly section of conditional code and refactors it into a few simple objects, bridging object-oriented theory and practice. The talk includes her take on the Gilded Rose refactoring kata and the idea that duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

Why HN recommends it: HN treats it as a top-tier programming talk for learning refactoring and for the wrong-abstraction principle, recommended repeatedly over a decade.

“this talk captures all the important values in a single example.” — HN comment, 2016

item.title: "Testing Distributed Systems w/ Deterministic Simulation" by Will Wilson
item.description:
Strange Loop Conference · talk · intermediate · evergreen

Will Wilson of FoundationDB explains how the team tested their distributed database using deterministic simulation. By running the whole system in a simulator with injected faults and reproducible seeds, they could find rare concurrency and network bugs.

Why HN recommends it: HN treats it as the canonical talk on simulation testing and a mind-blowing example of how far rigorous testing can go.

“this is one of the most amazing talks on distributed systems” — HN comment, 2018

item.description:
DevTernity Conference · talk · intermediate · evergreen

Ian Cooper's DevTernity talk revisits Kent Beck's original TDD ideas and shows where misunderstandings crept in. It argues tests should target behaviors through public interfaces rather than implementation details, so suites support refactoring instead of resisting it.

Why HN recommends it: HN repeatedly calls it the best talk on testing, and many say it changed how they approach tests, mocks and the meaning of a unit.

“This excellent talk completely changed the way I approached testing. Every developer who writes tests needs to watch this now!” — HN comment, 2021

Richard Feldman argues that functional programming is not the norm largely because of historical accidents, such as C++ popularity, platform exclusivity, marketing spend and network effects, rather than merit. He traces the history of how languages become mainstream.

Why HN recommends it: HN treats it as the standard answer to why FP isn't mainstream and why languages succeed.

“This talk by Richard Feldman is an excellent discussion about why Functional Programming is not the norm” — HN comment, 2021

item.title: Maybe Not - Rich Hickey
item.description:
ClojureTV · talk · intermediate · evergreen

Rich Hickey's Clojure/Conj 2018 keynote argues that Maybe/Option types and rigid type signatures are a poor way to model data that changes over time. He builds the case around optionality, schema growth and compatibility, and presents the ideas behind Clojure spec as an alternative.

Why HN recommends it: HN commenters send people to it whenever nulls, Maybe/Option or static typing come up, as a thoughtful dissent from the type-system orthodoxy that changes how some people model data.

“Rich Hickey's "Maybe Not" should be watched by anyone who thinks nulls/nils/undefineds are okay.” — HN comment, 2018

item.description:

Rafal Dittwald's Clojure/north talk shows how to move from writing Java-style code in Clojure to thinking in data-driven, functional terms. He walks through a JavaScript example, refactoring imperative code step by step into a functional core.

Why HN recommends it: HN repeatedly recommends it as a fantastic demonstration of procedural, OOP and FP approaches to the same problem, and of functional core and imperative shell.
